facts.value: Geometry is one of the oldest branches of mathematics, beginning with empirical recipes concerning shapes such as lines, angles, and circles.
The concept of proofs was introduced by the ancient Greeks, requiring every assertion to be proved.
Euclid systematized geometry around 300 BC in his book Elements.
Euclidean geometry is the study of shapes and their arrangements constructed from lines, planes, and circles in the Euclidean plane and three-dimensional Euclidean space.
Euclidean geometry remained unchanged until the 17th century when René Descartes introduced Cartesian coordinates.
Analytic geometry allows the study of curves unrelated to circles and lines, defined as the graph of functions or implicit equations, leading to differential geometry.
In the 19th century, mathematicians discovered non-Euclidean geometries, which do not adhere to the parallel postulate.

Today's subareas of geometry include projective geometry, affine geometry, differential geometry, manifold theory, Riemannian geometry, algebraic geometry, topology, algebraic topology, discrete geometry, convex geometry, and complex geometry.
